papers.title: UV-excited autofluorescence uncovers multicopy suppressors of a Cdc14-associated meiotic defect
papers.abstract: The Cdc14 phosphatase plays essential roles in meiotic chromosome metabolism and cell-cycle progression, yet the cellular pathways capable of compensating for reduced Cdc14 function remain poorly understood. To explore these connections, we performed a multicopy suppressor screen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, using a mutant CDC14 allele that severely impairs sporulation. UV-excited ascospore-wall autofluorescence enabled the rapid screening of approximately 14,400 transformants, while subsequent microscopy provided quantitative validation of sporulation phenotypes. Photographic image processing facilitated candidate recovery, and a complementary computational analysis of archived images established the reproducibility of fluorescence-associated detections across different acquisition conditions. Genetic screening and independent plasmid retransformation identified four genomic-library plasmids that reproducibly enhanced sporulation. Molecular characterisation of the strongest suppressors revealed genomic regions associated with chromatin regulation and nuclear-pore organisation. Further analysis prioritised two particularly promising candidate genes: RCO1, encoding a component of the Rpd3S histone-deacetylase complex, and POM34, encoding an integral membrane nucleoporin. Suppressor activity was retained in a reduced POM34-containing construct, strengthening its candidacy for further functional investigation. Together, these findings establish an effective fluorescence-guided strategy for multicopy suppressor discovery and reveal promising genetic connections between Cdc14-dependent meiotic progression, chromatin regulation and nuclear architecture.

papers.title: Genome survival and descent in population pedigrees
papers.abstract: Motivated by issues of the maintenance of genetic variation in a highly endangered species, we continue earlier studies into the population genetics ancestry and descent of genome segments. In this paper, we focus on the survival and descent of genome in a population pedigree of a diploid dioecious species. We consider a population potentially being maintained from a small founder base, taking the canonical example a random-mating population of 100 males and 100 females. We show how previous methods to examine the ancestry of a single genome in such a population can also be used to account the survival genetic lengths and number of descendant copies of founder genome segments, and explore the variance of these measures. We show the variance of the population distribution over realizations within a pedigree is scarcely smaller then the variance over pedigrees: variation is in meiosis rather than in pedigree. While all founders continue to lose genome over time, the very first generations are critical to determining the amount of surviving genome. Dependence among founders is slight, except for between the two genomes of a founder: however when monogamy is enforced this high dependence extends to founder mates. We briefly consider extensions of population size (both smaller and larger), of mating structure, and of variance in offspring number, including variance in male reproductive success.

papers.title: LAMP sheds light on how sequence to function models learn variant effects during post-training
papers.abstract: Genomic sequence-to-function (S2F) models show promise for interpreting noncoding genetic variation, yet they currently underestimate the effects of most causal variants. This leads to fine-mapping failures that are reflected in their underperformance relative to linear baselines at predicting gene expression across individuals from personal genome sequences. Improving personal genome predictions, which reflect this underestimation, is therefore critical. There is broad interest in post-training S2F models to improve these predictions, yet many groups have shown that doing so with personal genome sequences and paired expression values does not meaningfully improve predictions on held-out genes and people (HOGP). Why these post-training efforts to improve predictions on HOGP, and therefore causal variant underestimation, remains unclear. To understand why, we introduce LAMP (Learning of Artificial Motif Perturbations), a framework in which artificial SNVs (aSNVs) perturbing transcription factor motifs are substituted into personal genome datasets genome-wide with large, consistent, and causal effects on gene expression. These aSNVs are designed to be deliberately easy to learn, yet fine-tuning Enformer using this LAMP framework led to persistent underperformance on HOGP, which suggests fundamental challenges for learning variant effects during post-training that are independent of the complexity of natural genetic variation. Our findings suggest this underperformance is caused in part due to challenges learning to strengthen enhancer-gene links during post-training. In particular, models struggle with learning to rewire attention weights to relate aSNV detection, over distance, to a change in expression of the target gene. This limitation is caused by strong pre-trained priors that downweight distal regulatory elements, causing extreme data inefficiency in learning to attend to distal elements, and variants within them, during post-training. Second, sequence variability between loci containing different instances of the same TF motif obscures otherwise easy-to-learn motif perturbation patterns and also hinder learning of variant effects. Our results suggest that the scale of observed human genetic variation is vastly insufficient to maximize S2F model accuracy on HOGP via simple fine-tuning, consistent with past outcomes. We propose data augmentation strategies that, under LAMP, significantly improve learning of aSNV effects by strategically targeting the limitations we identified. We release LAMP as a tool to troubleshoot and optimize future S2F post-training objectives.

papers.title: Local GEBVs and additive variance in maize heterotic groups across low- and high-stress environments
papers.abstract: Hybrid maize (Zea mays L.) parents are chosen within heterotic groups. Drought and heat stress are expected to become more frequent, but little is known about how they change the additive variance of each group and where in the genome it lies. We analyzed testcross grain yield from 62 Genomes to Fields environments, classified as low or high stress by climate. For 1,362 parents from three heterotic groups and two doubled-haploid families, we fitted a genomic model with group deviations and calculated local genomic estimated breeding values in 164-kb segments. In the heterotic groups, high stress reduced additive variance by 4057%, and the genetic correlation between conditions was 0.730.99. Within groups, the distribution of variance across the genome was similar between conditions (correlation 0.841.00), and genotype-by-environment interaction was spread over many low-variance segments. Genome-wide association detected 25 loci under low stress and 18 under high stress, none shared, but half or more lay in high-effect, high-variance segments that were nearly the same in both conditions. The best possible cross between the two heterotic pools exceeded the best evaluated hybrid by 105117%, a gap that depended on segment size, not on stress. With 25 founders, stacking the best segments reached 9495% of the pool potential, versus 5692% for selection on total breeding value, whose founders were more related. Founders chosen in one condition reached, in the other, 94100% of the potential of those chosen there. Local breeding values can guide the choice of donors and founders under both conditions.

papers.title: Sequential co-translational assembly of the yeast SAGA DUB module precedes post-translational core docking.
papers.abstract: The 1.8-megadalton SAGA coactivator is organized into discrete functional modules, yet how individual catalytic modules are assembled and integrated into the holo-complex remains poorly understood. Here, we dissect the assembly pathway of the four-subunit histone H2B deubiquitinating (DUB) module in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Pairwise RIP-qPCR uncovers a unidirectional network of co-translational interactions sequentially linking Sus1, Sgf11, Ubp8, and Sgf73. Combining systematic deletion genetics with co-immunoprecipitation and quantitative NanoBiT assays in intact living cells, we demonstrate that these contacts form an obligate linear cascade rather than independent binary events: each upstream subcomplex licenses the next nascent-chain engagement, sustains downstream Sgf11 and Ubp8 stability, and precludes post-translational bypass. Conversely, DUB subunits exhibit no co-translational interactions with the SAGA core interface, indicating that completed modules dock post-translationally. Thus, unlike single-scaffold assembly models, SAGA separates multi-step co-translational module templating from post-translational holo-complex docking, safeguarding compositional fidelity.

papers.title: A single kindred across centuries: patrilineal continuity and a female-mediated increase in the local genetic component of the Lake Onega area at the Kondopoga cemetery
papers.abstract: We report the first genome-wide ancient DNA data from a medieval population in the territory of the modern Republic of Karelia, Russia: 1240K capture data for 22 individuals from the Kondopoga cemetery on Lake Onega, a churchyard used from the 12th to the 19th century. Combining relatedness estimates, autosomal and X-chromosomal identity-by-descent, uniparental lineages, burial position and archaeological dating, we place eight individuals in a single pedigree spanning five generations, anchored on a founding couple buried in the highest part of the cemetery. Identity-by-descent links almost all the remaining individuals to that couple, indicating that the sample is not a cross-section of a local population but a single kindred, which is the object of this study. Within it, the founding males paternal lineage recurs from the 12th-13th to the 16th century, mitochondrial lineages differ between individuals of the same generation, and autosomal ancestry shifts between generations rather than between archaeological phases. The ancestry of the founders is closest to populations from northwestern Rus and the eastern Baltic, while the Uralic-related ancestry entering the pedigree is best modelled using present-day Finnic groups of the region. The family was patrilineal, and its profile was reshaped by the women who married into it.

papers.title: TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) reveals histone profiles of activated neurons
papers.abstract: Epigenomic profiling methods such as CUT&RUN/Tag are commonly employed to evaluate the genomic localization of histone modifications, transcription factors, and chromatin regulating proteins. Numerous transgenic mouse models also exist that label specific cell populations by leveraging Cre-based recombination and fluorescent reporters to allow for cell type specific epigenetic profiling in vivo. However, none of these systems allow for rapid, parallel processing for cell-type-specific CUT&RUN/Tag. Here, we report the development of TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) in which we leverage a recombination-based system that results in conditional expression of a Sun1-GFP fusion protein with a TEV site introduced between Sun1 and GFP. Like the existing INTACT system, nuclei tagged by cell-type specific Cre recombinase activity can be efficiently purified using immunoprecipitation to allow for rapid, efficient, and in parallel nuclei isolation. However, with the addition of TEV protease, TIC-TaC nuclei can be subsequently removed from the beads allowing for downstream CUT&RUN/Tag. We applied this system to neurons isolated from the cortex to define the effects of seizure induced neuronal activation on numerous histone modifications and histone variant proteins and identified concordant shifts in H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H2A.Z and H2BE at seizure responsive genes. Together, through the development and application of TIC-TaC to allow for parallel processing of tissue for cell-type specific analysis, we uncover activity-dependent regulation of chromatin in the brain.

papers.title: The program STRUCTURE is good at detecting contemporary hybridization
papers.abstract: The program STRUCTURE is widely used in conservation genetics to detect human-caused hybridization between previously isolated populations. However, its performance at this specific task is not yet known, and methods used to interpret the model output vary widely among studies. We simulated hybridization between two populations on the timescale of real-world cases and tested STRUCTURE's ability to correctly detect hybridization based on a simple "hybrid signal": inferring the presence or absence of a minimum of one hybrid. Overall, this returned the correct result in 100% of scenarios when Fst between the two populations was between 0.05-0.15 when using an optimal Q-threshold of 0.10. Performance was slightly reduced when divergence was very weak (Fst = 0.01, with an optimal Q-threshold between 0.30-0.35) or when the population receiving migrants was substructured, but it still returned the correct result in 89-100% of cases, depending on simulation parameters. We conclude that STRUCTURE, paired with this hybrid signal and our recommended Q-thresholds, is an appropriate tool for detecting contemporary hybridization.

papers.title: sHSP-induced oligomerization enhances mammalian transcription factor potency
papers.abstract: Recently, a non-canonical role for small heat shock proteins (sHSPs) was identified, wherein sHSP-induced oligomerization drives targeted genomic accumulation of an endogenous silencing complex. Here we repurpose this property to develop sHSPs as compact, tunable tags for transcriptional engineering. Screening sHSPs across the tree of life, we show that sHSPs fused to transcription factors (TFs) can increase on-target genomic occupancy, recruit sHSP-tagged proteins, and amplify target-gene activation in mammalian cells. Distinct sHSPs vary in levels of transcriptional occupancy and output, providing a means to tune TFs activity while maintaining targeting specificity. This work establishes sHSPs as a new class of compact (~20kDa), tunable, activity-enhancing tags with broad potential for transcriptional engineering and synthetic biology.

papers.title: Sequencing of the Prnp-Prnd deletion junction in Prn-/- mouse tissues after formaldehyde fixation and >22 years at room temperature.
papers.abstract: In 2004, Nicolas Genoud and colleagues reported that deletion of Prnd, which encodes Doppel, prevented neurodegeneration in mice with extensive Prnp deletions. The work tested the proposal that abnormal Doppel expression in the brain caused cerebellar degeneration in mice lacking the cellular prion protein, PrP. Advances in automated image analysis have expanded scrutiny of published figures, and post-publication reviews have raised concerns about apparent figure manipulation in this work, calling its authenticity and reliability into question. Here we assemble the surviving contemporaneous records of the original work and report new experiments on archived tissue. To reassess the reported genetic rearrangement, DNA from archived paraffin-embedded brain tissue was amplified across the putative deletion junction and analyzed by bidirectional Sanger sequencing and comparison with mouse reference sequences. The two reads spanned 607 positions and placed Prnp-side sequence, a 34-base loxP site and Prnd-side sequence in the expected order, with 93 intervening bases that matched bacteriophage P1 loxP-flanking and plasmid cloning-site sequences rather than the mouse reference and therefore probably derive from the targeting construct. Independent de novo reassembly from the 2025 Sanger chromatogram files reproduced the junction sequence; the assemblies differed only at three terminal bases with low base-call quality. These findings support the expected local junction arrangement and provide a publicly inspectable sequence description that extends the molecular information presented in the original paper. The amplicon size and the position of the loxP site match the values stated in the original paper, as does the approximately 18-kb distance between the two flanking sequences in the wild-type genome, which the deletion brings together. Recovery of junction DNA after more than two decades of room-temperature storage as paraformaldehyde-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue demonstrates the value of retained material for reassessing historical experimental claims.

papers.title: Population-aware computational assessment of base-editing accessibility among pathogenic variants on human chromosome 21: an African-ancestry-focused pilot study
papers.abstract: Background Population-aware gene-editing research requires independent evaluation of clinical variant evidence, ancestry-stratified allele observations, nucleotide correction chemistry, and sequence-level editing constraints. We developed a source-traceable chromosome 21 pilot connecting these dimensions without equating computational accessibility with therapeutic editability. Methods Reviewed ClinVar pathogenic/likely pathogenic single-nucleotide variants were matched by GRCh38 chromosome, position, REF and ALT to overall and African/African-American (AFR) gnomAD v4.1 exome allele counts. Exploratory frequency contrasts used two-sided Fisher exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Higher-confidence variants with canonical adenine or cytosine base-editing chemistry underwent NGG PAM/editor-window screening, bystander enumeration, MANE v1.5 consequence annotation, theoretical joint-product assessment and chromosome 21-restricted guide-homology searches. Results Among 1,944 ClinVar variants, 851 matched gnomAD; 694 were quality-filtered and alternate-allele-observed overall, including 300 higher-confidence records. Six variants met exploratory AFR-elevation criteria. Of 234 higher-confidence ABE/CBE chemistry-compatible variants, 118 (50.4%) had at least one nominal NGG/PAM-window placement, 55 (23.5%) a nominal zero-bystander placement, and 44 (18.8%) a zero-bystander placement without an additional chromosome 21 NGG near-match within three mismatches. The 261 placements generated 295 hypothetical bystander events (195 distinct alleles); five distinct potential products overlapped pathogenic/likely pathogenic ClinVar alleles. Across placements, 764 theoretical target-corrected sequence states were enumerated, of which 503 contained at least one bystander. Three variant-level editing-accessibility comparisons between AFR-observed and AFR-unobserved alleles were not statistically significant (BH q=1.0). Conclusions Canonical correction chemistry substantially overestimates nominal local base-editor accessibility. A population-aware, transcript-informed computational framework can identify hypotheses for follow-up, but allele-frequency contrasts, guide-similarity results and enumerated sequence products do not establish clinical efficacy, experimental editing specificity or genome-wide off-target safety.

papers.title: Language-Driven Clustering of Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence & Recovery Studies for Forensic Activity-Level Evaluation
papers.abstract: Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence, and Recovery (TPPR) data are essential for forensic activity level evaluations (ALE); however, concerns remain regarding the accessibility of relevant literature. This study investigated whether automated literature retrieval and natural language processing (NLP) methods could be used to identify and characterize TPPR studies. Existing forensic repositories were combined with records retrieved through the Web of Science Application Programming Interface (API) and enriched with bibliographic metadata, producing a corpus of 3,279 unique records. Automated retrieval tools were evaluated, and transformer-based topic modeling was applied to examine the breadth of the literature. The results showed that database APIs provided the most reliable mechanism for literature retrieval, while topic modeling identified meaningful groupings corresponding to major forensic disciplines and trace evidence types. The findings indicate that TPPR literature exists and that automated methods can support its discovery and organization. Although the availability of literature does not necessarily imply suitability for ALE, the results suggest that the principal challenge is the discovery, assessment, and reuse of published studies rather than their absence. Automated retrieval, semantic search, and quality assessment frameworks may improve access to relevant evidence and support the development of forensic knowledge systems for evaluative reporting and Bayesian network construction.

papers.title: Unravelling the hidden diversity of the monkfish Lophius gastrophysus using integrative taxonomy
papers.abstract: The monkfish Lophius gastrophysus is a commercially exploited demersal species distributed along the continental shelf and slope of the western Atlantic Ocean. Like other anglerfish species, L. gastrophysus has a pelagic larval stage that can facilitate dispersal by oceanic currents (Farina et al., 2008). It is considered the most widely distributed species in the genus, spanning more than 10,000 km of the western Atlantic Coast, from North Carolina to Argentina. Previous morphological analyses based on a limited set of traits suggested that L. gastrophysus may comprise two distinct species. We tested this hypothesis by combining molecular and morphometric data. Sequence data were obtained from 38 L. gastrophysus individuals collected from Northern and Southern American populations. We also used a subset of 13 specimens for geometric morphometrics. Phylogenetic analyses and automatic species delimitation methods consistently distinguished Northern and Southern Atlantic L. gastrophysus as separate clades, and geometric morphometrics supported the same split. The congruence among geographic, molecular, and morphometric data indicates that L. gastrophysus harbours two distinct lineages, highlighting the need for a formal taxonomic revision and separate fisheries management of northern and southern Atlantic populations.

papers.title: Is the Bitter Lesson coming to genomic prediction? An untuned tabular foundation model matches or beats specialized methods
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) is dominated by models designed around assumptions about how genetic variation affects phenotypes. Here we asked how well a general-purpose pretrained tabular foundation model called TabPFN-3.5 does with no genetics-specific modeling and no tuning when given marker genotypes directly. We benchmarked TabPFN-3.5 using a published comparison of 18 GP methods on 18 traits in six plant species. Against the published means, TabPFN-3.5 ranked first on 11 of 18 traits and had the best median rank. Because the published benchmark did not identify its test sets, we reran GBLUP, RKHS and elastic-net models on the same splits as TabPFN-3.5. Against the best of these, TabPFN-3.5 was significantly behind on only one trait, spruce wood density, and ahead on 12 of 18, with significant gains on all three soybean traits and rice flowering time. In the soybean panel, which had the largest number of lines, its advantage was clearest. In leave-families-out cross-validation, where models were trained on some soybean families and used to predict lines from other families withheld from training, every model lost accuracy and TabPFN-3.5 performed on par with GBLUP and RKHS. That a general-purpose learner matches or exceeds decades of specialized GP models is consistent with Sutton's Bitter Lesson, which holds that methods that scale with computation eventually overtake those built on human knowledge of the domain.

papers.title: Pigmentation markers enable efficient co-CRISPR selection in the pantry moth Plodia interpunctella
papers.abstract: CRISPR co-targeting (co-CRISPR) of pigment genes facilitates the identification and recovery of genome-edited individuals in model organisms. Using Plodia interpunctella, an emerging lepidopteran model, we characterized mutant phenotypes of eight genes involved in the melanin and ommochrome biosynthesis pathways (black, ebony, yellow, tan, vermilion, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase/cinnabar (kmo/cn), scarlet, and white) to evaluate their suitability as co-CRISPR markers. Disruption of black, ebony, and yellow altered larval sclerite, pupal cuticle, and adult wing coloration. All four ommochrome pathway genes studied contributed to larval cuticle and adult eye pigmentation, whereas only vermilion and kmo/cn disruption produced visible phenotypes in the adult wings. Sequencing revealed low apparent mosaicism in some yellow and tan G0 individuals, along with recurrent deletions at the yellow and tan target sites consistent with possible microhomology-mediated end joining repair. Using white or scarlet as co-CRISPR selection markers, we identified G0 individuals carrying a secondary mutation in the yellow gene with a positive predictive value of 100% by scoring its knockout phenotype. Extending this approach to six meiosis-related genes without visibly scorable phenotypes, selection based on the white mutant phenotype identified sequence-confirmed mutations at the corresponding gene-of-interest in 191 of 206 G0 individuals (93%). Together, these findings establish white and scarlet as effective co-CRISPR selection markers and provide a practical strategy for facilitating functional genetic studies in Plodia.

papers.title: Genetic diversity of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium malariae and its association with infectivity of Anopheles coluzzii in the Mfou Health District, Central Region of Cameroon
papers.abstract: Background Malaria remains a major public health challenge in Cameroon, with sustained transmission particularly in forest-savannah transition zones. Although Plasmodium falciparum is the predominant malaria parasite, non-falciparum species such as P. malariae also contribute to the human infectious reservoir and to onward transmission. Parasite genetic diversity and multiplicity of infection (MOI) are recognized determinants of malaria transmission and may influence the prevalence and intensity of infection in mosquito vectors. However, whether parasite genetic diversity and MOI differentially influence the infectivity of P. falciparum and P. malariae to local Anopheles coluzzii populations remains poorly characterized. This knowledge gap is particularly relevant in the Mfou Health District, where malaria transmission persists and both P. falciparum and non-falciparum infections occur. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted between September 2022 and November 2023 in twelve primary schools in the Mfou Health District. Finger-prick blood samples were collected from children aged 3-17 years and examined by microscopy to identify Plasmodium infections and gametocyte carriers. Gametocyte-positive participants were enrolled in direct membrane feeding assays (DMFA) using locally reared Anopheles coluzzii. Blood samples were tested under two conditions: whole blood (WB) and replacement with naive AB serum. Mosquito infection outcomes were assessed at the oocyst (day 7) and sporozoite stages (day 14). Parasite species were confirmed by quantitative PCR (qPCR), and genetic diversity was assessed using seven microsatellite loci, together with msp1 and msp2 markers for P. falciparum and pmmsp1 for P. malariae. MOI and expected heterozygosity (He) were calculated, and their associations with mosquito infection prevalence and intensity were evaluated using generalized linear models. Results Among 2,807 children screened, 2,111 (75.2%) were infected with Plasmodium, and 388 (18.4%) carried gametocytes. A total of 169 children aged 4-13 years were selected for membrane feeding assays using Anopheles coluzzii, of whom 68% successfully infected mosquitoes. Among 10,872 dissected mosquitoes, 20.2% were infected at the oocyst stage, with both infection prevalence and intensity being higher in mosquitoes fed on AB serum-reconstituted blood than with whole blood. Sporozoite-stage infections were detected in 5.8% of mosquitoes, predominantly under AB serum conditions. Mosquito infection prevalence and intensity increased with gametocyte density, although submicroscopic gametocyte carriers were also infectious. P. falciparum exhibited high genetic diversity (MOI 2.4 {+/-} 0.8; He 0.72 {+/-} 0.07), while P. malariae showed limited diversity (MOI 0.11-0.21; He {approx} 0). Mixed-species and polyclonal infections were associated with enhanced infection outcomes. Moreover, the msp2 FC27 allelic family in P. falciparum and the 800-bp pmmsp1 allele in P. malariae were associated with oocyst development. Overall, parasite genetic diversity, multiplicity of infection, and species composition were positively associated with mosquito infectivity, with only minor seasonal variation observed. Conclusion Malaria transmission in Mfou is sustained by genetically diverse and multiclonal P. falciparum infections, with P. malariae also contributing to the human infectious reservoir. The association of parasite genetic diversity, MOI, and allele-specific factors with mosquito infectivity underscores the importance of addressing asymptomatic and multiclonal infections in malaria control strategies.

papers.title: LRPPRC gene replacement therapy preserves cardiac function and prevents premature death in a mouse model of mitochondrial disease
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in LRPPRC disrupt mitochondrial gene expression, causing severe and incurable mitochondrial disease with neurological involvement accompanied by hepatopathy or cardiomyopathy. The development for gene therapy for LRPPRC-linked disease is hindered by the large LRPPRC coding sequence exceeding AAV cargo capacity when combined with classical regulatory elements. Here, we engineered compact single rAAV9 vectors expressing human or mouse LRPPRC and administered them intravenously to heart and skeletal muscle-specific Lrpprc knockout mice. This approach restored cardiac LRPPRC expression, preserved oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) function, prevented cardiomyopathy and markedly extended survival. While skeletal muscle rescue was partial, the therapy effectively prevented fatal cardiac dysfunction. These findings provide the first in vivo proof-of-concept that AAV-mediated LRPPRC gene replacement can preserve OXPHOS function and prevent lethal cardiomyopathy, supporting its potential as a therapeutic strategy for mitochondrial disease linked to LRPPRC deficiency.

papers.title: Additive genes underlie Mendelian inheritance and contribute to heterosis
papers.abstract: Mendel proposed the laws of segregation and independent combination in his study. However, he focused on "dominant" characters but left "intermediate" ones. Using genotypic and phenotypic data for four representative genes, we reveal connections between the "intermediate" and "dominant" characters. We demonstrate that the fundamental inheritance patterns of these genes are additive effects on both component and compound traits. Additive effects involving more than two genes generate non-additive effects in hybrids. For compound traits such as grain yield, their inheritance depends on differential patterns of component traits in parents; only parents with optimal balances of reciprocal differences in component traits produce overdominant effects, which is important for hybrid breeding.

papers.title: Continuous ancestry profiles from genomes and genealogies
papers.abstract: Using a single population label to represent an individual's ancestry may offer convenience, but ancestry is multidimensional, continuous, and reflects contributions from multiple ancestral sources. Here, we demonstrate empirically that ancestry profiles outperform categorical ancestry labels in capturing this complexity. Relatedness among 28,332 genotyped individuals was measured using haplotype painting and ordination and was regressed on regional ancestry proportions from the deep genealogies available for one-third of the cohort. When tested on participants in a validation set, predicted profiles placed 78% of documented ancestry in the correct region, against 48% for the training set average. Giving each participant a single regional label placed only 32% of their documented ancestry correctly, and a perfect classifier naming each person's largest documented region would reach only 38%, because most individuals carry ancestry from several regions. Thus, the continuous profile captures substantially more ancestry than any classification, providing support for representing ancestry as a continuum rather than a label.

papers.title: Plasmodium vivax relapse reservoirs in Ethiopia: microhaplotype sequencing informs recurrent infection origins
papers.abstract: Determining the origin of recurrent Plasmodium vivax infections is critical for quantifying the public health burden of the hypnozoite reservoir, understanding transmission potential, and evaluating anti-relapse antimalarial efficacy. In Ethiopia, P. vivax is a major contributor to malaria burden, but the relative contribution of relapse to recurrent infections remains poorly quantified. We performed microhaplotype genotyping using a panel of 93 genome-wide markers and applied a probabilistic recurrence classification framework to recurrent P. vivax samples collected in two Ethiopian radical cure trials (IMPROV and OPRA). Genotyping was conducted on parasite isolates collected at enrolment and subsequent recurrences, with participants monitored over a 12-month follow-up period (IMPROV: 604 samples from 444 participants; OPRA: 621 samples from 342 participants). Recurrent infections were classified using a Bayesian hierarchical model implemented in Pv3Rs, which estimated marginal posterior probabilities of relapse, reinfection, or recrudescence based on genotyping data and background population dynamics. Priors were structured across biologically motivated time windows reflecting the natural history of P. vivax infection in Ethiopia and anticipated drug efficacy. Recurrences with a probability of relapse (p(L)) [≥] 0.75 were classified as relapses. In the absence of primaquine, probable relapse was the dominant classification for primary recurrent infections in both trials (75.5%; 102/135) and for consecutive recurrent infections within individuals (75.2%; 204/271). Primaquine substantially reduced the proportion of participants experiencing recurrent infections attributable to probable relapse, from 57.3% to 1.7% in IMPROV and from 60.2% to 9.5% in OPRA. Polyclonal infection at enrolment was independently associated with increased odds of recurrence and a higher rate of probable relapse in OPRA, with a consistent but non-significant trend observed in IMPROV. These findings provide direct molecular evidence that the hypnozoite reservoir is the dominant driver of recurrent P. vivax infections in Ethiopia in the absence of radical cure. The marked reduction in probable relapse following primaquine treatment highlights the critical importance of expanding access to safe and effective radical cure strategies in Ethiopia and other comparable high-transmission settings.

papers.title: Assembly-independent measurement of human Yq12 heterochromatin reveals population-scale variation and Yq12-derived RNA in testis
papers.abstract: Despite advances in long-read sequencing and telomere-to-telomere assembly, population-scale analysis of large satellite arrays remains challenging. Human Yq12 is a megabase-scale heterochromatic region composed primarily of DYZ1/HSat3A6 and DYZ2/HSat1B repeats, whose near-equal proportions are maintained despite extensive variation in total array length. Here, using complete Y-chromosome assemblies, we developed k-mer-based tools to estimate Yq12 size directly from short- and long-read sequencing data without requiring sample-specific complete assemblies. Across 1,597 males from the 1000 Genomes Project, Yq12 length ranged from ~1 to 52 Mb (mean 26.5 Mb) and varied substantially within and between Y haplogroups. Phylogenetic analyses supported long-term constraint of total Yq12 length near an equilibrium of 26 Mb and strongly coupled evolution of DYZ1 and DYZ2 around near-parity composition. In 303 father-son pairs, fathers had longer estimated Yq12 regions in 70.6% of pairs, while sons more often showed DYZ1:DYZ2 ratios closer to 1:1. Testis Iso-Seq identified transcripts containing DYZ1 and DYZ2 satellite sequences, while single-cell RNA-seq revealed their expression in haploid spermatids. These results establish a scalable framework for studying Yq12 population variation, intergenerational dynamics, and transcription, providing new opportunities to investigate how extreme satellite-array variation relates to Y-chromosome evolution and male germ-cell biology.

papers.title: Genetic ancestry influences the relative expression of ancestral haplotypes within admixed individuals
papers.abstract: Allele-specific expression (ASE) reflects differences between the two haplotypes a person carries, but most ASE studies have been done in European-descent samples. Admixed individuals carry haplotypes from different ancestral backgrounds within the same cell, which allows ancestry effects on regulation to be measured directly. We integrated phased whole-blood RNA-seq with local ancestry inference in 779 participants from the MAGENTA cohort, including non-Hispanic White, African American, Caribbean Hispanic, and Peruvian individuals. Higher West African (YRI) ancestry proportion was associated with more ASE-positive genes per person, and the association remained after adjusting for age, sex, Alzheimer's disease status, APOE genotype, and the number of heterozygous genes. Peruvian ancestry showed no significant association. A gene-level test of imbalance across population groups found 2,053 of 15,008 genes with significant differences, including the major histocompatibility complex in all four groups. A genome-wide scan of 2,213 1 Mb windows compared people carrying two haplotypes of different ancestries with those carrying two of the same ancestry. It identified 52 non-redundant loci that replicated across all four population groups, containing 201, 60, and 110 ancestry-associated genes under the CEU, YRI, and PEL reference baselines. A haplotype-resolved directional analysis showed no genome-wide advantage for either ancestry. It found locus-specific dominance at 11 loci, and only chr8:2-3 Mb (CSMD1) showed the same direction in more than one population group. Genetic ancestry therefore shapes allelic regulation at global, gene, and locus scales.

papers.title: Cell type-specific coexpression networks funnel genetic risk into core genes
papers.abstract: Genetic effects on common disease are mediated through many genes in multiple cell types, yet how networks connect genome-wide genetic risk to core disease genes remains unclear. One key limitation is that disease-related gene networks are likely cell type-specific, but these are poorly captured by bulk and pseudobulk coexpression networks. Here we used population-scale single-cell immune transcriptomes to decompose interindividual gene coexpression into cell type-shared and -specific networks, which have nearly opposite properties. Shared network hubs were enriched in constrained housekeeping genes, whereas cell type-specific hubs were dynamically expressed, rapidly evolving, and enriched in cell type-matched enhancers and transcription factors. Specific hubs enriched for immune disease GWAS heritability, Mendelian genes, and drug targets; these enrichments were absent or weak for non-immune disease and shared hubs. Gene-gene network edges enriched for causal trans regulation identified by trans eQTLs and perturb-seq, with shared hubs skewed to upstream regulators and specific hubs skewed to downstream disease-proximal genes. Specific hubs increased the relative success of genetically supported immune drug targets from 1.7-fold to 2.7-fold; for example, the lupus drug target BAFF is a monocyte hub connected to the Mendelian gene TREX1 and interferon-responsive genes. Overall, accounting for shared housekeeping networks reveals that cell type-specific networks funnel genetic risk into downstream and dynamic core disease genes.

papers.title: Extending Mendelian randomisation to founder-haplotype data in Diversity Outbred mice
papers.abstract: Observational associations can reflect confounding or reverse causation, which Mendelian randomisation (MR) avoids by using genetic variation to estimate causal effects. In Diversity Outbred (DO) mice such estimates can be tested experimentally, but applying human summary-data MR, with one scalar association per variant, ignores the differing effects of their eight founder haplotypes. We introduce Founder GLS-IVW, which uses each locus's founder-effect pattern for causal estimation and diagnosis. At Qsox1, it recovered the direction of effect seen in knockout mice, which one scalar coding failed to detect. Across 4,596 trait pairs, scalar and founder analyses disagreed for 29.7%; in seven of eight, only the founder analysis found an effect, using information scalar coding discards. Because exposure and outcome may be measured in different or partly overlapping animals, the method supports two-sample MR across separate experiments. Our R package qtl2mr, built on the widely used R/qtl2, helps prioritise mechanistic experiments.

papers.title: Pangenome Discoveries from Clinical Long-Read Genomes in Underrepresented Populations with Neurodevelopmental Disorders
papers.abstract: Genetic diagnoses remain elusive for many individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), and the gap is wider in populations poorly represented in genomic reference resources. To demonstrate the equitable advantage of long-read whole genome sequencing (LR-WGS) and pangenomes in terms of clinical utility, we analyzed 211 NDD cases and 107 unaffected relatives from 24 populations, integrating their assemblies, resulting in a total of 1204 haplotypes with the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 (HPRC_r2) and the Arab Pangenome Reference (APR) datasets. Clinical interpretation of small variants and structural variants (SVs) revealed pathogenic or likely pathogenic findings in 38.9% of the cases (82/211), and our workflow further detected pathogenic repeat expansions in 3.8% of the cases and runs of homozygosity (ROHs) exceeding 300 Mb in 4.7% of the cases, revealing substantial autozygosity suggestive of strong inbreeding. Beyond these clinical assessments, pangenome analysis revealed 3.9 million population-level novel small variants, 39,782 SVs and an average of 2.17 Mb of novel sequence per individual absent from linear references and global pangenomes. We identified 85.9 kb of case-unique nonreference sequences in exonic segments overlapping with curated NDD gene sets. Graph-based tertiary analysis further identified rare exonic complex homozygous rearrangements in the NDD associated genes for 2.4% of the cases. Together, these findings emphasize how diverse genome assemblies extend variant discovery beyond established linear reference-based clinical interpretation.

papers.title: Male-specific genome sequences for non-invasive sex identification in Nishikigoi (Cyprinus carpio)
papers.abstract: Nishikigoi, ornamental cultivars of the common carp (Cyprinus carpio), are economically valuable aquaculture teleosts in which mature females command significantly higher market prices due to superior body conformation and coloration. Consequently, early and non-invasive sex identification is highly desirable for commercial breeding. Although sex determination in common carp follows an XX/XY system, sex-chromosome-specific markers and field-applicable diagnostic methods for Nishikigoi have remained limited. In this study, we conducted sequence-based bulked segregant analysis using whole-genome shotgun sequencing of female and male pools in Kohaku, a representative Nishikigoi lineage. We identified male-specific candidate contigs and successfully developed PCR-based male-specific markers. Validation across multiple Nishikigoi varieties and wild common carp demonstrated that primary primer pairs achieved high diagnostic accuracy. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that these candidate contigs mapped to the genomic region on chromosome 25B containing the male-determining gene Pangu, with the primary marker located in immediate physical proximity to the gene. To enable field diagnostics, we combined non-invasive epidermal mucus DNA extraction, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), and chromatography-printed array strip (C-PAS) technology, establishing a rapid on-site detection workflow. Overall, this study provides highly reliable PCR markers associated with the sex-determination locus and establishes a non-invasive, field-applicable diagnostic platform to streamline commercial Nishikigoi breeding and sex-selected stock management.

papers.title: Integrated exome-transcriptome analysis of a schizophrenia case with an exceptionally low polygenic risk score
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia liability reflects both common polygenic variation and rarer variants of larger effect. We investigated a post-mortem schizophrenia case (SZ07) with a schizophrenia polygenic risk score below the first percentile among ancestry-matched cases, asking whether individual-level genomic and transcriptomic analyses could help identify potentially novel schizophrenia-relevant variants. We used exome analysis with multiple variant-prediction tools to generate a panel of variants and corresponding candidate genes potentially implicated in the pathological process in SZ07. The prioritised variants were then assessed using RNA sequencing of three cortical regions. Of these, only an IZUMO4 splice-acceptor variant showed direct RNA-level support. Beyond variant-specific analyses, we characterised broader transcriptomic abnormalities in the SZ07 brain. Pathway analysis of gene-level expression deviations implicated innate immune processes, calcium signalling, synaptic biology, and axon remodelling. Notably, compared with conventional single-sample biological pathway analysis, the analysis we used showed only a weak association with neuronal specificity, suggesting their reduced sensitivity to the main axis of variation related to cellular composition in bulk brain tissue gene expression data. Although the candidate genes showed no significant pathway-level convergence, the broader transcriptomic profile revealed coherent biological alterations largely compatible with the documented history of cerebrovascular disease in SZ07. These results demonstrate how the integration of exome and transcriptome data at the individual level enables the formulation and constraint of hypotheses regarding patient-specific genetic features and their molecular consequences, while highlighting important limitations related to tissue composition, comorbidity, and the choice of reference cohort.

papers.title: A genetic screen to identify host factors required for commensal bacterial adherence to the gut epithelia
papers.abstract: Bacterial adherence to gut epithelial cells likely involves host genetic components. We isolated a gut commensal bacterium, Lelliottia jeotgali, that can robustly colonize C. elegans through attachment to intestinal epithelial cells. Here, we developed a novel screen in C. elegans to identify host genes required for microbiome bacterial colonization. Using transgenic L. jeotgali strain expressing tdTomato, we conducted forward genetic screens in C. elegans to select for mutants that completely lost colonization. We identified multiple allelic mutations in five different C. elegans genes, termed knockout of Lelliottia adherence (kola) mutants, with a near complete loss of adherence. Each of kola-1-5 is uncharacterized and predicted to encode for a secreted or membrane-bound protein. We also identified gly-5, a GalNAc transferase that initiates O-linked glycosylation. Overall, we describe the first C. elegans screen to identify host factors that control microbiome bacterial colonization in the gut.

papers.title: Deciphering the Dynamics of Leukemogenic Transformation from Clonal Hematopoiesis in Congenital Neutropenia
papers.abstract: Inherited neutropenia syndromes, severe congenital neutropenia (CN) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), confer a high cumulative risk of MDS and AML. It is not yet clear which somatic mutations, in which combination, allele frequency and sequence identify patients at high risk. We analyzed clonal hematopoiesis (CH) in the largest representative cohort of inherited neutropenia patients to date - 658 samples from 309 patients - using error-corrected panel sequencing with longitudinal sampling. This was complemented in selected cases by single-cell DNA sequencing and genotyping of single-cell derived colonies. CH was detected in early childhood, affecting 37.7% of CN and 60% of SDS patients. The somatic mutation burden remained essentially unchanged over decades. In CN, CSF3R mutations were dominant across genetic subtypes, while additional mutations were rare and included ASXL1, TET2, and DNMT3A. ASXL1 mutations most frequently co-occurred with CSF3R mutations. Co-occurring CSF3R and TP53 mutations were only found in SRP54-CN and CLPB-CN patients. In SDS, TP53 was the most frequently mutated gene, followed by low-prevalence somatic mutations in DNMT3A, IDH1, PTPN11, and RUNX1. In CN-MDS/AML, RUNX1 and SETBP1 mutations emerged shortly before progression to MDS/AML, and membrane-proximal CSF3R mutations only at the leukemic stage. In SDS, biallelic TP53-mutant clones expanded prior to transformation, and a variant allele frequency (VAF) of dominant TP53 clone above 0.074 discriminated between patients who progressed and those who did not. Peripheral blood reflected bone marrow genotype for most key drivers. Leukemic transformation in inherited neutropenia is therefore not stochastic, but rather follows a defined mutational sequence, initiated in childhood.
